issues.legal_issue: Co-landlords with different eligibility for a special eviction procedure may jointly choose the forum when their shared eviction claim is maintainable in either forum.
material_facts: A widow and her two adult sons jointly sought eviction of tenants from non-residential premises for the sons’ business needs.
The widow belonged to a category eligible to use the special procedure before the rent authority, while the sons did not.
The pleaded business requirements provided a common cause of action for the co-landlords.
issues.conclusion: The joint proceedings before the Rent Controlling Authority were competent and maintainable; the co-landlords could instead have chosen to file a civil suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 23-A(b) and 23-J of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, a qualifying landlord may seek eviction through the special procedure for a qualifying non-residential business need. Sections 12(1)(f), 11-A and 45 govern the ordinary civil-court route and the forum’s jurisdiction. A co-owner may sue for eviction without joining other co-owners if they do not object: Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, Kanta Goel v. B.P. Pathan and Pal Singh v. Sunder Singh. The presence of additional proper parties does not change the essential character of a proceeding: Messrs. Importers and Manufacturers Ltd. v. Pheroze Framroze Taraporewala. The court also relied on Shivraj Jat v. Asha Lata Yadav and Harbans Singh v. Margrat G. Bhingardive, and on the principles that a plaintiff is dominus litis, that a right must have a remedy, and that multiplicity of proceedings should be avoided; see also Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar.

rule.if: joint_eviction_claim and common_requirement_of_co_landlords and (some_co_landlords_qualify_for_special_forum and some_co_landlords_do_not)

predicates.joint_eviction_claim: Co-landlords jointly brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.common_requirement_of_co_landlords: The pleaded need for eviction supplied a cause of action shared by the co-landlords bringing the claim.
predicates.some_co_landlords_qualify_for_special_fo: At least one co-landlord belongs to a class eligible to use a special eviction procedure.
predicates.some_co_landlords_do_not: At least one co-landlord bringing the joint claim does not belong to a class eligible to use that special procedure.

issues.definition: When co-landlords jointly bring an eviction claim based on a shared requirement and differ in eligibility for a special forum, they may choose either forum available for the claim.

issues.legal_issue: A bona fide non-residential business requirement is established when the evidence supports the claimed business needs and the absence of suitable alternative accommodation owned by the landlords.
material_facts: One shop was sought for an adult son to start a business, and another was sought for an adult son to continue a business then conducted in rented premises.
The Rent Controlling Authority and the High Court evaluated the evidence and found the requirements proved.
The landlords had no suitable alternative non-residential accommodation of their own.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the concurrent findings that the landlords had proved their bona fide requirements.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23-A(b) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act permits eviction where non-residential premises are bona fide required for the landlord’s business or that of a major son or unmarried daughter, subject to the absence of other reasonably suitable non-residential accommodation of the landlord’s own. In the special procedure, the requirement is presumed bona fide unless the tenant proves otherwise. The assessment of bona fides is objective; once bona fides are established, the landlord’s subjective choice among available premises is respected. The Court relied on Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Mahesh Chand Gupta for the assessment of alternative accommodation and bona fide need.

rule.if: special_eviction_proceeding and nonresidential_business_need and evidence_supports_genuine_need and no_suitable_owned_alternative

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant through a special proceeding for a claimed bona fide requirement.
predicates.nonresidential_business_need: The premises were sought for starting or continuing a non-residential business of the landlord or an eligible family member.
predicates.evidence_supports_genuine_need: The evidence, assessed by the decision-maker, supports the asserted business requirement as genuine.
predicates.no_suitable_owned_alternative: The landlord has no other reasonably suitable non-residential accommodation of the landlord’s own in the relevant locality.

issues.definition: In a special eviction proceeding, a supported genuine need for non-residential business premises, together with the absence of a suitable owned alternative, establishes a bona fide business requirement.

issues.legal_issue: Alternative premises do not defeat a bona fide non-residential eviction claim unless they are owned by the landlord and reasonably suitable for the claimed use.
material_facts: The landlords had obtained possession of other premises, but those premises were rented rather than owned by them.
The tenant also pointed to space on the first floor, which was used partly as a godown and partly for stitching garments; the claimed business premises were ground-floor shops.
There was no evidence that first-floor shops in the market attracted business comparable to ground-floor shops.
issues.conclusion: The rented premises were irrelevant as alternatives, and the first-floor space was not reasonably suitable to defeat the claim for the ground-floor shops.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(1)(f) and 23-A(b) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, an alternative must be the landlord’s own accommodation and reasonably suitable for the claimed non-residential use. Suitability is assessed in comparison with the premises from which eviction is sought; an available alternative may undermine bona fides if it is suitable and is unreasonably refused. Once bona fides are established, the landlord’s subjective choice among accommodations is respected. The Court relied on Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Mahesh Chand Gupta.

rule.if: bona_fide_eviction_claim and alternative_accommodation_exists and (alternative_is_not_owned or alternative_is_not_reasonably_suitable)

predicates.bona_fide_eviction_claim: A landlord seeks eviction on a bona fide requirement for non-residential premises.
predicates.alternative_accommodation_exists: The tenant identifies other premises that might be available to the landlord.
predicates.alternative_is_not_owned: The identified premises are not owned by the landlord.
predicates.alternative_is_not_reasonably_suitable: The identified premises are not reasonably suitable for the claimed use when compared with the premises sought.

issues.definition: An identified alternative does not defeat a bona fide eviction claim if it is not owned by the landlord or is not reasonably suitable for the claimed use.
